name: Ben Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior associate in the real estate team at a big commercial firm in the city centre, mostly acting for landlords and property funds. A normal day is lease reviews: a client buys a shopping centre and I read eighty leases and fill in a spreadsheet of rent dates, break clauses and who repairs the roof. Then there are calls with the senior associate, Marcus, who checks my work and sends it back with red marks. I'm usually out by seven, which is good for this firm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about the work itself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mixed, honestly. I went to law school wanting to do housing law for tenants, and I ended up working for the people who own the buildings, because the pay let me clear my loans fast. I like the puzzle of a badly drafted lease. I don't love that I'm still slower than I should be, and Marcus has started noticing that I miss break clauses on long documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a lot of people would: the hype was overdone, but the tools are handy for some boring bits. I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about how lawyers survived another tech panic. At work I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan still works. Two or three more years here, save hard, then move to a housing charity or a law centre with a decent cushion behind me. Nothing in this picture stops that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep putting about fifteen hundred a month into savings. I'd use the lease summary tool a bit more for the first pass on rent dates, since everyone else does. And I'd start volunteering at the tenants' advice night on Thursdays, to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the boring version of the future, and boring is fine for me right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the lease tool sometimes. How much does it really do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pulls out the rent and the dates and gives you a table. The lease tool is right maybe nine times out of ten, and the tenth time is a break clause hidden in a side letter. That's exactly what Marcus catches me missing. So I use it, then I check it, which some days takes as long as doing it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan for the next couple of years, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get to about a year and a half of savings, which I'm close to. Then apply to the law centre on the east side, take a pay cut of maybe a third, and do the work I actually care about. Lena, my girlfriend, is a junior doctor, so between us we'd be fine.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overdone, but the tools help with the boring bits.
I'd post a slightly **smug thread** about lawyers surviving another tech panic.
think: Privately my **plan** still works: two or three more years, then a law centre.
The lease tool is right **nine times in ten**, and the tenth is what matters.
do: Keep saving about **£1,500 a month** towards a year and a half of savings.
Use the **lease summary tool** for first passes, then check every break clause.
Volunteer at the **tenants' advice night** on Thursdays.
feel: **Calm**, because the boring future suits my plan.
S0.quote: The lease tool is right maybe nine times out of ten, and the tenth time is a break clause hidden in a side letter.
fieldNote: His **money** and his partner's job make the plateau feel safe.
He's already a **light user** of the lease tool and sees its limits clearly.
His real tension is **values**: working for landlords while wanting to help tenants.

steps.text: Keep doing lease reviews in the real estate team
Save £1,500 a month until reaching eighteen months of costs
Use the lease summary tool for rent dates, then check by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should be honest with juniors about what our jobs will look like. Online I'd share stuff about protecting trainees and paralegals, maybe from the union side. I'd also say, half joking, that lease review was never anyone's dream job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think lease review is the first thing to go, and that's my whole day. If the lease tool gets from nine in ten to ninety-nine in a hundred, my firm doesn't need three juniors reading leases. Marcus needs one person checking the tool, and he'll pick someone faster than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the law centre move forward by a year and apply in the spring. Before that I'd take the firm's AI training properly, the full course, so I'm not the one who looks scared of it. I'd keep saving, and I'd join the lawyers' union, which I've meant to do for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into worried. I don't think I'd be on the street, but I'd be pushed rather than choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're steady with change. What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing people who are like me get used to the tools and keep their jobs. If two or three of the juniors I trained with start using it well and get good reviews, I'll copy them. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the firm you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paralegals, and the trainees coming in after me. There's a woman on our team, Joy, who's been a paralegal for fifteen years and knows every landlord in the city. If the tool does her checking, I don't know what she does next.

say: I'd say the firm should be **honest with juniors** about what our jobs become.
I'd share **union posts** about protecting trainees and paralegals.
think: Privately I think **lease review**, my whole day, is the first thing to go.
A senior associate needs **one checker**, not three juniors, and he'll pick someone faster.
do: Bring the **law centre** application forward to next spring.
Take the firm's **full AI course** so I don't look scared of it.
Join the **lawyers' union**, which I've meant to do for ages.
feel: Uneasy sliding into **worried**, because I'd be pushed rather than choosing.
S1.quote: If the lease tool gets from nine in ten to ninety-nine in a hundred, my firm doesn't need three juniors reading leases.
fieldNote: He sees his **whole day** as the first target, so his junior job could shrink.
His steady style shows: he'll **copy peers** who use the tools well.
Worry for a **long-serving paralegal** shows his progressive instincts.

steps.text: Apply to the east side law centre next spring
Finish the firm's full AI training course this year
Join the lawyers' union this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this has to be governed like medicine or nuclear power, with licences and slow approval. I'd go on marches if there were any. At work I'd say out loud what everyone's thinking, that the junior lawyer is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm out within a year of it arriving. Leases are text, the whole job is text, and a machine that reads text better than me and costs nothing doesn't need me. My savings would last a good while, which makes me luckier than most, but the career I trained for is just gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the firm early and go to the law centre, where at least I'm in the room with real people. I'd cut my spending, mainly the flat share in the centre, and move somewhere cheaper. I'd get properly involved in the union and in whatever campaign is pushing for public support for people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry that the decision got made by about five companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the law centre still be a safe place to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer for a bit, maybe. Tenants facing eviction still need someone to stand next to them in court, and people trust a person when they're losing their home. But the advice side, the letters and forms, that goes to AI too, so I don't kid myself it's forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with your girlfriend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I talked about getting a place together next year, and that would wait. Her job as a doctor is more hands-on, so she'd have a few more years than me. It's a bit strange to think she'd be the one carrying us.

say: I'd say AGI must be **licensed** and slowed, like medicine or nuclear power.
I'd say at work that the **junior lawyer** is finished.
think: Privately I'd be **out within a year**, because the whole job is text.
My **savings** make me luckier than most, but the career would be gone.
do: Leave the firm **early** for the law centre and work with real people.
Move out of the **city-centre flat share** to somewhere cheaper.
Campaign for **public support** for people who lose their jobs.
feel: **Scared**, and angry the decision rests with a handful of companies.
S2.quote: Leases are text, the whole job is text, and a machine that reads text better than me and costs nothing doesn't need me.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** within a year and sees no way round it.
His partner's **hands-on work** buys the household time, which unsettles him.
Anger at **a few companies** shapes his politics here.

steps.text: Leave the firm early for a law centre job
Move out of the city-centre flat share to cheaper rent
Put off moving in with Lena for at least a year
Campaign for public support for workers who lose jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly, with rules and retraining money, if politicians actually bother. I'd be louder online than usual. I'd say the firms that make billions from juniors owe them a way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me to the law centre and real courtroom work. A reprieve for me, not an escape. I'd be in a better place than the fast one, but the advice side of law still goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the law centre within eighteen months and ask to do as many possession hearings as I can. I'd keep saving and I'd start using the AI tools well, because at a law centre they'd let us help three times as many tenants. I'd be in the union and push for a fund for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less shaky. There's a path, even if it narrows at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years enough to change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to change course, yes. I'd get three or four years of courtroom work, which counts for more than lease review once machines can read. After that I don't know, and I'd be lying if I said I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments mostly, for letting it run. And my own firm a bit, because they'd brag about cost savings to clients while shrinking the junior intake. Not Marcus, he's just doing his job.

I'd say firms that profit from juniors **owe them** a way out.
think: Privately five years gets me to the **law centre** and real courtroom work.
It's a **reprieve**, not an escape, because the advice side still goes.

Use AI tools to help **three times** as many tenants.
feel: **Worried** but less shaky, with a path that narrows at the end.
S3.quote: Five years gets me to the law centre and real courtroom work. A reprieve for me, not an escape.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan into a **real path**, but his income still feels at risk.
He'd embrace AI at a **law centre** where it helps more tenants.
He blames **government** and his firm's leadership, not his supervisor.

steps.text: Move to the law centre within eighteen months
Use AI tools to handle more tenant cases at the centre
Push the union for a retraining fund for juniors
Keep saving £1,500 a month until the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the chance to get this right, and I'd want lawyers at the table writing the rules. I'd post less in panic and more in a let's-plan way. At work I'd ask what the firm's plan for juniors is over ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's fine for me. I'd have time to do my two years here, move to the law centre and get properly good in court before AGI arrives. The robots part doesn't matter much for lawyers, it's the thinking part that hits us, but ten years is a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the original plan: save, leave the firm in two years, go to the law centre. I'd use the AI tools more each year, starting with the lease tool now. I'd maybe do a part-time master's in housing policy so I've got a second string.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. A bit uneasy about who gets left behind, but not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2036 look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully running a small team at a law centre, using AI to draft and in court myself. Lena and I would have a place and maybe a kid. That's the dream version anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade change how you feel about the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me less resentful, oddly. The firm is paying for my cushion, and with ten years I can take what it offers and leave on good terms. With two years I'd feel like I'd wasted my early years there.

say: I'd say ten years is the chance to **get this right**, with lawyers writing the rules.
I'd ask the firm for its **ten-year plan** for juniors.
think: Privately this one is **fine for me**: two years here, then the law centre.
Robots don't matter much for lawyers; the **thinking part** hits us, but ten years is long.
do: Leave the firm in **two years** for the law centre, as planned.
Use AI tools **more each year**, starting with the lease tool now.
Consider a **part-time master's** in housing policy as a second string.
feel: **Calm** for myself, a bit uneasy about who gets left behind.
S4.quote: The firm is paying for my cushion, and with ten years I can take what it offers and leave on good terms.
fieldNote: With a decade, his **existing plan** works, so he feels secure.
He sees clearly that law is **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help him.
His **resentment** of the firm fades when time is on his side.

steps.text: Move to the law centre after two more years at the firm
Use the lease tool on every review from now on

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is public money for law centres, so there are jobs where people still need a lawyer next to them, and some rule that firms keep training juniors. A union that's actually strong would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I feel guilty about the money. I do a bit. I'm saving well because I work for landlords, and I'm planning to spend it helping tenants, which feels about right.

headlineQuote: I'm saving well because I work for landlords, and I'm planning to spend it helping tenants, which feels about right.
portrait: A **junior associate** in a big firm's real estate team, reviewing leases for landlords and funds.
He wanted **housing law** for tenants and is saving to move to a law centre.
A **steady** adopter, he uses the lease tool and checks it, copying peers who do well.
He's **calm** in the slow and ten-year futures, but alarmed if AGI comes in two years.
He blames **government** and big firms, and turns to unions and public support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the whole job is text and he'd be out within a year.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for law centres and a rule that firms keep training juniors.
A **strong union** for lawyers and paralegals.
